notes.h: Glycolysis: splitting glucose in five stages (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Respiration starts with glycolysis, a short pathway that partly breaks down glucose before the cell knows whether oxygen is available. It is the first stage of both aerobic respiration (with oxygen) and anaerobic respiration (without oxygen).
points: Glycolysis means 'sugar splitting'. It takes place in the cytoplasm (cytosol, the fluid part of the cell outside the organelles), is controlled by about ten enzymes working in sequence, and needs no oxygen.
1. Activation: two ATP molecules are used to add phosphate groups to the glucose (C₆, a six-carbon sugar). This makes the glucose more reactive, so it is an investment of energy that is repaid later.
2. Splitting: the six-carbon sugar is split into two three-carbon molecules.

3. Oxidation: hydrogen, as electrons and protons, is removed from each three-carbon molecule by dehydrogenase enzymes and picked up by NAD⁺ (a carrier molecule that accepts hydrogen), forming NADH. Two NADH are made per glucose.
4. ATP generation: four ATP are made as phosphate groups are transferred to ADP. Net gain: 4 made minus 2 used, so 2 ATP per glucose.
5. Product: two molecules of pyruvate (pyruvic acid, C₃) per glucose. Pyruvate still holds most of the energy of the glucose, which is why much more energy can be released from it later.
Summary: glucose + 2 ADP + 2 Pi + 2 NAD⁺ → 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP (net) + 2 NADH. No CO₂ is released in glycolysis, because the carbons all stay in the two pyruvate molecules.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name the first stage of respiration, where it happens (cytoplasm), its product (pyruvate, a 3-carbon molecule) and its net ATP gain. The net gain is 2 ATP, not 4, because two ATP are spent at the start. Glycolysis releases no CO₂, and it needs no oxygen.

notes.h: Where glycolysis occurs and what enters it (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Glycolysis is the most widespread pathway in living things, and it is not limited to glucose from food.
points: Glycolysis happens in almost every living cell, prokaryotic (no nucleus) and eukaryotic (with a nucleus). This suggests it evolved early in the history of life, before there was oxygen in the atmosphere, which fits with it needing no oxygen.
Other six-carbon sugars, such as fructose, and the glucose from glycogen or starch enter the same pathway.
notes.tip: Glycolysis needs no oxygen but it also happens in aerobic respiration, so don't call it 'the anaerobic stage only'. It is the first stage in both.

notes.h: Transfer molecules in glycolysis (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Two transfer molecules, ATP and NAD⁺, carry energy and hydrogen through glycolysis. How each one is used explains why the cell must have a way to carry on without oxygen.
points: ATP: two are used to activate the glucose and four are made by transferring phosphate from the sugar molecules directly to ADP. The net 2 ATP is all the energy anaerobic respiration releases per glucose.
NAD⁺: the cell has only a small supply. Glycolysis converts NAD⁺ to NADH, so glycolysis stops if NADH is not turned back into NAD⁺, because there would be no NAD⁺ left to accept hydrogen.

The fate of NADH depends on oxygen. With oxygen, it passes its electrons to the electron transport chain in the mitochondrion (the organelle where the second stage of respiration happens). There is more on this in Second-stage process.
Without oxygen, NADH passes its hydrogen to pyruvate instead, a process called fermentation. Either way, NAD⁺ is regenerated, so glycolysis can carry on.
notes.tip: A common exam question is how fermentation lets glycolysis continue. The answer is that NADH is converted back to NAD⁺, which glycolysis needs in order to keep running.

notes.h: Fermentation: regenerating NAD⁺ without oxygen (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Without oxygen, the mitochondrion cannot take up NADH's hydrogen, so NAD⁺ would run out and glycolysis would stop. Fermentation solves this problem, and it works in the cytoplasm.
points: When oxygen is absent or too scarce, pyruvate is not passed to the mitochondrion. Instead, in the cytoplasm, NADH passes its hydrogen to pyruvate, or to a product made from it. This regenerates NAD⁺, so glycolysis can keep running and keep making its 2 ATP per glucose.
The purpose of fermentation is to regenerate NAD⁺, not to make more ATP. No ATP is made after glycolysis.

Lactic acid fermentation, in animal muscle cells and in lactic acid bacteria such as those used to make yogurt: pyruvate (C₃) takes hydrogen from NADH and becomes lactic acid (lactate, C₃). This is one step, and no CO₂ is released.
Overall for lactic acid fermentation: glucose → 2 lactic acid, with a net 2 ATP.

Alcoholic (ethanol) fermentation, in yeast and in plant cells short of oxygen, such as waterlogged roots: pyruvate (C₃) first loses one carbon as CO₂, forming a two-carbon compound. This then takes hydrogen from NADH and becomes ethanol (C₂).
Alcoholic fermentation is two steps, with one CO₂ released per pyruvate. Overall: glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂, with a net 2 ATP.
Lactic acid has three carbons, like pyruvate; ethanol has two, because one carbon is lost as CO₂.
notes.tip: Fermentation makes no extra ATP. Students often say lactic acid formation 'releases energy', but its job is to regenerate NAD⁺. Learn the products: yeast make ethanol and CO₂, human muscle makes lactic acid.

notes.h: Which product, when, and why so little energy (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Whether fermentation happens, and what it produces, depends on the organism and on the conditions. Fermentation also releases far less energy than aerobic respiration.
points: The product depends on the organism's enzymes. Animals and many bacteria make lactic acid, while yeast and plants make ethanol.

Whether fermentation happens at all depends on conditions. Yeast and muscle respire aerobically when oxygen is available and switch to fermentation when it is not. There is more on the conditions in Investigation: conditions for fermentation.
Fermentation releases little energy because glucose is only partly broken down. Lactic acid and ethanol still contain much of the original energy; ethanol is a fuel, for example in biofuels.

Diagram: flow chart. Glucose (C₆), 2 ATP used, 4 ATP made, 2 NAD⁺ → 2 NADH, gives 2 pyruvate (C₃). Branches: (a) oxygen: mitochondrion; (b) no oxygen, animals, some bacteria: lactic acid (C₃); (c) no oxygen, yeast, plants: CO₂, ethanol (C₂). NADH → NAD⁺ loops to glycolysis. Label cytoplasm, mitochondrion.
notes.tip: If asked which 3-carbon molecule enters the mitochondrion, the answer is pyruvate. Without oxygen it stays in the cytoplasm and is fermented.

keyTerms.definition: The first stage of respiration, in the cytoplasm, which converts one six-carbon glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules, with a net gain of 2 ATP and no oxygen.
The three-carbon product of glycolysis, which goes to the mitochondrion when oxygen is present or is fermented when it is not.
The reduced form of NAD⁺, which carries hydrogen from glycolysis to the electron transport chain or to pyruvate in fermentation.
Converting NADH back to NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue; this is the purpose of fermentation.
The conversion of pyruvate to lactic acid by NADH, with no CO₂ released, in animal muscle and lactic acid bacteria.
The conversion of pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂ by NADH, in yeast and plant cells short of oxygen.

questions.prompt: Name the first stage of respiration, state where it occurs in the cell, and name its three-carbon product.
questions.model: The first stage of respiration is glycolysis. It takes place in the cytoplasm (cytosol) of the cell. Its three-carbon product is pyruvate (pyruvic acid).

questions.prompt: Describe glycolysis, with reference to the role of ATP and NAD⁺.
questions.model: Glycolysis splits one six-carbon glucose molecule into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm, without oxygen. Two ATP are used at the start to activate the glucose, and four ATP are made as phosphate is transferred to ADP, giving a net gain of 2 ATP. NAD⁺ accepts hydrogen from the three-carbon molecules and is converted to NADH; two NADH are made per glucose. Glycolysis needs a supply of NAD⁺, so NADH must be converted back to NAD⁺ for it to continue.

questions.prompt: Explain why yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide while human muscle produces lactic acid when oxygen is scarce, and explain why fermentation is necessary for the cell.
questions.model: Yeast and muscle cells have different enzymes. In yeast, pyruvate first loses one carbon as CO₂, forming a two-carbon compound, which then takes hydrogen from NADH to become ethanol. In human muscle, pyruvate takes hydrogen from NADH in one step to become lactic acid, so no CO₂ is released. Fermentation is necessary because, when oxygen is absent, NADH cannot pass its electrons to the electron transport chain. NADH passes its hydrogen to pyruvate instead, which regenerates NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can keep running and keep making its 2 ATP per glucose. Fermentation does not make more ATP.
